expeditions.title: Shadow Detectives
expeditions.question: How does a shadow change during a day?
expeditions.materials: Paper, pencil, ruler, a fixed outdoor object visible from a safe spot
steps: Sketch the object's shadow and record the time without looking at the Sun.
Return to the same spot twice later and measure its shadow.
Compare lengths and directions while keeping the object fixed.
expeditions.evidence: A table of three times, lengths and sketches.
expeditions.explanation: Earth's rotation changes the Sun's apparent position, so a fixed object's shadow changes. Clouds can make its edge uncertain.
expeditions.extension: How would the results differ on another day?
expeditions.safety: Never look at the Sun or use optical equipment to view it. Stay on safe ground with an adult.
expeditions.duration: Three brief observations across one day

expeditions.title: Moon Journal
expeditions.question: Does the Moon look the same every evening?
expeditions.materials: Notebook, pencil, safe window or outdoor view
steps: Record the date, time and a sketch of the Moon when visible.
Repeat on five evenings; write not visible when clouds or timing prevent a sighting.
Compare the lit shapes without inventing missing observations.
expeditions.evidence: Five dated entries including gaps.
expeditions.explanation: The Moon's phases reflect changing views of its sunlit half. A cloudy night is missing evidence, not a new phase.
expeditions.extension: What would a longer observation period reveal?
expeditions.safety: Observe from a safe place with an adult; do not walk in the dark while looking upward.

expeditions.title: Cloud Watch
expeditions.question: How much does the sky change in fifteen minutes?
steps: Draw the visible sky using a window frame as your boundary.
Repeat after five and fifteen minutes.
Describe changes in cloud coverage, shape and movement.
expeditions.evidence: Three labeled sketches and one question.
expeditions.explanation: Clouds can move and change shape; a short view cannot establish a long-term weather pattern.
expeditions.extension: Would observers facing another direction report the same sky?
expeditions.safety: Stay indoors during storms; never look directly at the Sun.

expeditions.title: Rock Evidence
expeditions.question: Can visible features help us sort rocks without naming them?
steps: Sketch each stone and describe color, texture and visible layers.
Sort them using one stated rule.
Ask a partner to apply your rule, then refine it if necessary.
expeditions.evidence: A labeled sorting key and a record of disagreements.
expeditions.explanation: A classification is useful when another observer can apply it. Appearance alone may not identify a rock reliably.
expeditions.extension: Which feature would need a closer observation?
expeditions.safety: Use clean stones already collected with permission; do not break, taste or collect from protected places.

expeditions.title: Leaf Patterns
expeditions.question: What similarities and differences can we observe in fallen leaves?
expeditions.materials: Fallen leaves or drawings, paper, pencil
steps: Choose three leaves and draw their outlines and veins.
Compare length, edges and vein patterns using the same descriptors.
Group them and explain one leaf that is difficult to place.
expeditions.evidence: Three drawings and a grouping explanation.
expeditions.explanation: Careful descriptions separate observations from guesses about plant identity.
expeditions.extension: Would your grouping work for three new leaves?
expeditions.safety: Use known safe fallen leaves with adult help; avoid unknown plants and wash hands.

expeditions.title: Seed Water Watch
expeditions.question: How does access to water affect a seed's early growth?
expeditions.materials: Two clear containers, paper towels, large bean seeds, water
steps: An adult sets up equal seeds on two towels, moistening only one.
Keep both in the same location and sketch daily for five days.
Compare changes and note any seeds that did not behave alike.
expeditions.evidence: Daily drawings with water conditions labeled.
expeditions.explanation: Seeds need suitable conditions to germinate; one small trial cannot tell us what every seed will do.
expeditions.extension: What would you keep constant in a repeat trial?
expeditions.safety: Do not eat experimental seeds. Adults discard any moldy material without opening it near faces; wash hands.

expeditions.title: Evaporation Marks
expeditions.question: Where does water in an uncovered cup go?
expeditions.materials: Two identical unbreakable cups, water, paper cover, pencil
steps: Add equal water amounts and mark each starting level.
Cover one cup loosely with paper and leave the other open in the same safe place.
Compare levels daily for several days.
expeditions.evidence: Starting and final water-level sketches.
expeditions.explanation: Liquid water can enter the air as water vapor. A cover can change air movement, but spills or different temperatures can also affect results.
expeditions.extension: How could you distinguish a spill from evaporation?
expeditions.safety: Keep cups away from electronics and pets; do not drink the experiment water.

expeditions.title: Condensation Clues
expeditions.question: Where do droplets outside a cold cup come from?
expeditions.materials: Two unbreakable cups, cool water, room-temperature water, cloth
steps: Dry both cups and fill one with cool water and one with room-temperature water.
Watch the outsides without splashing.
Record where droplets appear and compare with your prediction.
expeditions.evidence: Drawings of both cup surfaces and room conditions.
expeditions.explanation: Water vapor in the surrounding air can condense on a sufficiently cold surface; visible droplets depend on conditions.
expeditions.extension: Would the result change in drier air?
expeditions.safety: An adult handles cold water; wipe spills promptly and keep away from electronics.

expeditions.title: Dissolving Detective
expeditions.question: Does stirring change how quickly salt seems to disappear?
expeditions.materials: Two clear cups, room-temperature water, salt, spoons, timer
steps: Use equal water and salt amounts in both cups.
Stir one at a steady pace and leave the other still.
Record visible grains at equal time intervals.
expeditions.evidence: A time table using visible grains as the observation rule.
expeditions.explanation: Dissolving disperses salt in water; disappearing from sight does not mean the salt ceases to exist.
expeditions.extension: What could make the comparison unfair?
expeditions.safety: Use small kitchen quantities with adult supervision; do not taste experimental mixtures.

expeditions.title: Floating Predictions
expeditions.question: Can size alone predict whether an object floats?
expeditions.materials: Bowl, shallow water, three waterproof household objects
steps: Predict which objects will float and explain your reasoning.
Place each gently in shallow water and record the result.
Compare a prediction that worked with one that needs revising.
expeditions.evidence: A prediction-and-result table.
expeditions.explanation: Floating depends on the object's average density and the fluid, not simply how large it looks.
expeditions.extension: Could the same material behave differently if its shape changed?
expeditions.safety: An adult chooses objects too large to swallow; keep water away from devices and empty the bowl afterward.

expeditions.title: Paper Absorbency
expeditions.question: Which paper carries water farther in the same time?
expeditions.materials: Paper towel, writing paper, tissue, shallow tray, ruler
steps: An adult prepares equal-width strips of each paper.
Dip equal lengths into shallow water at the same time.
Measure the wet region after one minute and repeat with fresh strips.
expeditions.evidence: Two trials with material names and wet lengths.
expeditions.explanation: Water can move through spaces in paper. Thickness, coatings and fiber structure can affect the result.
expeditions.extension: Would measuring water held give the same ranking?
expeditions.safety: Work over a tray; keep wet paper away from electrical equipment.

expeditions.title: Surface Friction
expeditions.question: How do surfaces change a toy's sliding distance?
expeditions.materials: Low cardboard ramp, block, cloth, smooth paper, ruler
steps: Release the block from the same marked ramp position onto smooth paper.
Repeat three times, then replace the landing surface with cloth.
Measure each stopping distance without pushing the block.
expeditions.evidence: Six distances and a comparison of their spread.
expeditions.explanation: Contact between surfaces can resist motion. Repeated measurements help separate a pattern from a single unusual run.
expeditions.extension: What other variable could alter stopping distance?
expeditions.safety: Use a low floor-level ramp, a soft block and a clear landing area.

expeditions.title: Gentle Ramp Motion
expeditions.question: How does a low ramp's height affect travel?
expeditions.materials: Cardboard ramp, large toy car, books, ruler
steps: Release the car without pushing from a marked point on a low ramp.
Repeat three times and measure travel beyond the ramp.
Raise the ramp slightly and repeat on the same surface.
expeditions.evidence: Two sets of distances and a description of the change.
expeditions.explanation: Changing height changes the energy available to motion; wheels and floor friction also affect travel.
expeditions.extension: Would a different car produce the same distances?
expeditions.safety: Keep the ramp on the floor, below knee height, and clear the path.

expeditions.title: Sound Vibrations
expeditions.question: Can we see something vibrate while hearing it?
steps: Hold most of the ruler firmly on the table with a short end overhanging.
Gently pluck the free end and watch its motion.
Try a different overhang and describe the sound without claiming an exact frequency.
expeditions.evidence: Drawings of two setups and descriptive sound notes.
expeditions.explanation: Vibrations can produce sound. Changing the free length changes how the ruler vibrates.
expeditions.extension: What would you need to measure pitch precisely?
expeditions.safety: Use an uncracked flexible ruler and gentle motion; keep faces away and sound comfortable.

expeditions.title: Distance and Sound
expeditions.question: How does a quiet sound change with distance?
expeditions.materials: Paper, pencil, partner, clear indoor space
steps: A partner taps a table gently at a steady loudness.
Listen from three marked distances in the same room.
Compare descriptions and list possible distractions or echoes.
expeditions.evidence: Three distance notes and one uncertainty.
expeditions.explanation: Sound spreads and interacts with surroundings. Personal loudness descriptions are not calibrated measurements.
expeditions.extension: How could a wall or doorway change the comparison?
expeditions.safety: Keep sound quiet; no headphones or loud alarms. Stop if uncomfortable.

expeditions.title: Light Through Materials
expeditions.question: Which materials let an LED flashlight's light pass?
expeditions.materials: LED flashlight, paper, thin cloth, clear plastic lid
steps: Shine the flashlight through each material onto the same wall.
Keep distance and room lighting similar.
Sort the results as clear transmission, diffuse transmission or little visible transmission.
expeditions.evidence: A material table with sketches of the light patches.
expeditions.explanation: Materials transmit, scatter or absorb light differently; these categories describe this setup rather than every possible thickness.
expeditions.extension: Would two layers change a material's category?
expeditions.safety: Use only an LED flashlight, never lasers or sunlight; do not shine into eyes.

expeditions.title: Reflection Route
expeditions.question: Can you redirect a flashlight beam toward a target?
expeditions.materials: LED flashlight, unbreakable mirror, paper target
steps: Place the target on a table and predict a mirror position.
Shine the flashlight at the mirror and adjust it gently.
Sketch the incoming and outgoing paths for two successful positions.
expeditions.evidence: Two labeled path sketches.
expeditions.explanation: A mirror changes light's direction; the geometry depends on its orientation.
expeditions.extension: How would moving the target change your setup?
expeditions.safety: Adult supervision; use an unbreakable mirror and keep reflected light below faces.

expeditions.title: Bent Pencil Mystery
expeditions.question: Why can a pencil look displaced at a water surface?
steps: View a pencil in an empty cup from the side.
Add water and observe from the same position.
Change viewing angle and draw the apparent bend or displacement.
expeditions.evidence: Three labeled observations.
expeditions.explanation: Light changes direction when passing between air and water. The pencil's appearance can change without the pencil bending.
expeditions.extension: What observation would show the pencil itself is still straight?
expeditions.safety: Use a shallow cup on a stable tray and wipe spills.

expeditions.title: Pebble Shadow Map
expeditions.question: How can lighting imitate changes in terrain?
steps: Draw the stone's surface under light from the left.
Keep the stone still and move the light to the right.
Mark which apparent features changed and which remained identifiable.
expeditions.evidence: Two sketches with light direction arrows.
expeditions.explanation: Shadows can hide or emphasize surface features. Comparing images requires attention to illumination.
expeditions.extension: What should accompany a photograph used as evidence of change?
expeditions.safety: Use a clean stone and LED flashlight; avoid eyes.

expeditions.title: Habitat From a Window
expeditions.question: What living things use a small patch of ground?
steps: Choose a patch visible without entering it.
Observe for ten minutes on three occasions and tally visible visits.
Separate what you saw from what you think an animal was doing.
expeditions.evidence: Three dated tallies and one uncertainty.
expeditions.explanation: Observation effort and time of day affect what is detected. Not seeing an organism does not prove absence.
expeditions.extension: What would a different observation time reveal?
expeditions.safety: Do not approach, feed or handle wildlife; keep exact nest locations private.

expeditions.title: Wind Clue Log
expeditions.question: Can everyday clues reveal changing wind?
expeditions.materials: Window view, notebook, safe view of a flag or leaves
steps: Select one visible indicator such as a flag.
Record its movement at three times without assigning an unmeasured speed.
Compare with a second visible indicator.
expeditions.evidence: Time-stamped descriptions and a comparison.
expeditions.explanation: Different objects respond differently to wind; an observation can indicate movement without measuring speed.
expeditions.extension: What instrument would help quantify your observations?
expeditions.safety: Observe indoors in bad weather; never attach objects near roads or power lines.

expeditions.title: Soil Settling
expeditions.question: What separates when a soil-water mixture rests?
expeditions.materials: Clear plastic container with lid, garden soil, water, spoon
steps: An adult adds a small amount of known clean garden soil to water and closes the lid.
Gently swirl, then leave still.
Sketch the mixture immediately, after ten minutes and the next day.
expeditions.evidence: Three timed layer sketches.
expeditions.explanation: Particles can settle at different rates. Layers alone do not identify every mineral or prove the water is safe.
expeditions.extension: Which particles remained suspended longest?
expeditions.safety: Adult setup; no contaminated soil, tasting or opening near faces. Wash hands and dispose outdoors responsibly.

expeditions.title: Air Has Space
expeditions.question: Can trapped air keep a paper towel dry?
expeditions.materials: Plastic cup, paper towel, shallow bowl of water
steps: An adult secures dry towel inside the bottom of a cup.
Push the inverted cup straight into shallow water, then lift it straight out and inspect.
Repeat while gently tilting and compare.
expeditions.evidence: Dry-or-wet observations for both orientations.
expeditions.explanation: Air occupies space; tilting lets it escape and can allow water farther into the cup.
expeditions.extension: What observation tells you air escaped?
expeditions.safety: Adult handles water; use plastic containers, small water amounts and a tray.

expeditions.title: Two Eyes, Two Views
expeditions.question: Does changing viewpoint change an object's apparent position?
steps: Hold a pencil at comfortable arm's length.
Close one eye, then the other, without moving the pencil.
Draw its apparent position against the background and repeat at another distance.
expeditions.evidence: Two pairs of sketches.
expeditions.explanation: Different viewpoints can shift an object's apparent position against a background; this is a parallax effect.
expeditions.extension: How might distance affect the apparent shift?
expeditions.safety: Keep the pencil point down and away from faces; skip closing eyes if uncomfortable.

expeditions.title: Fair Test Workshop
expeditions.question: Which parts of an investigation must stay the same?
expeditions.materials: Paper, two paper-ramp designs, soft block, ruler
steps: Write a question about ramp surface and a predicted result.
List starting point, slope and block as things to keep the same; run three trials per surface.
Explain one limitation and redesign the test.
expeditions.evidence: A plan, six measurements and a revised plan.
expeditions.explanation: Changing one factor at a time makes interpretation easier, but repeated trials and honest limitations remain important.
expeditions.extension: What result would make you change your explanation?
expeditions.safety: Use low floor-level ramps and clear the landing area.

expeditions.title: Signals in the Sky
expeditions.question: What can an aircraft observation tell us, and what remains uncertain?
expeditions.materials: Notebook, safe sky view; optional adult-operated flight map
steps: Open the existing ELS Signals in the Sky field notes linked below.
From a safe place, record the time and describe one aircraft or record that none was visible.
Compare direct observations with any map information and label each source.
expeditions.evidence: An observation, its source and an explanation of a mismatch or missing information.
expeditions.explanation: A digital map and a direct sighting provide different evidence; neither should be treated as a complete picture.
expeditions.extension: What could explain an aircraft missing from a map?
expeditions.safety: Never observe while driving, enter restricted areas or point lights at aircraft. Adults handle online maps; keep exact home coordinates private.

expeditions.title: Human Robot Instructions
expeditions.question: How precise must instructions be for another person to follow them?
steps: Draw a small tabletop grid and mark a start and finish.
Write move and turn commands for a partner moving a marker.
Watch without correcting them mid-run, then revise ambiguous commands.
expeditions.evidence: An original command list, observed error and corrected list.
expeditions.explanation: An algorithm is a sequence of instructions. Testing exposes assumptions the author may not notice.
expeditions.extension: Can someone else follow the revised version without help?
expeditions.safety: Use a tabletop marker rather than blindfolded walking.

expeditions.title: Loop the Pattern
expeditions.question: When can repeated instructions be shortened?
steps: Write commands to draw a red-blue-blue pattern three times.
Replace the repeated block with a repeat-three-times instruction.
Ask a partner to draw from each version and compare.
expeditions.evidence: Two equivalent instruction lists and drawings.
expeditions.explanation: A loop expresses repeated work without writing every repetition; its boundaries must be clear.
expeditions.extension: What changes if the repetition count is zero?
expeditions.safety: Use age-appropriate pencils; do not place small supplies in the mouth.

expeditions.title: Branching Trail
expeditions.question: Can a decision rule respond to different inputs?
expeditions.materials: Paper cards, pencil, large colored shapes
steps: Write a rule: if a shape has three sides, move it left; otherwise move it right.
Test six shapes, including one ambiguous drawing.
Revise the rule or drawing and explain what changed.
expeditions.evidence: An input-output table and revised rule.
expeditions.explanation: A conditional chooses an action based on a test. Ambiguous inputs need a defined response.
expeditions.extension: How would you add a second condition without confusing the first?
expeditions.safety: Use large paper shapes; an adult handles any cutting.

expeditions.title: Bug Hunt
expeditions.question: How can one wrong instruction change a route?
steps: Design a five-command route and test it.
Replace one command deliberately and give the route to a partner.
Ask them to find the first divergence and repair only that command.
expeditions.evidence: Correct route, faulty route and repair explanation.
expeditions.explanation: Debugging compares expected behavior with observed behavior and narrows down the cause.
expeditions.extension: Could two different bugs produce the same final position?
expeditions.safety: Keep the activity on paper; no real navigation is involved.

expeditions.title: Binary Lanterns
expeditions.question: How can on-off choices represent numbers?
steps: Face selected cards upward and sum their values.
Represent every whole number from zero to fifteen.
Challenge a partner to decode three arrangements.
expeditions.evidence: A table of values and card states.
expeditions.explanation: Four binary positions can represent sixteen distinct patterns; the agreed place values give those patterns numerical meaning.
expeditions.extension: What extra values become possible with a 16 card?
expeditions.safety: Use large cards; no electrical components required.

expeditions.title: Pixel Message
expeditions.question: How can a grid store a small picture?
steps: Draw an eight-by-eight picture using two colors.
Encode each row as eight zeros and ones with a color key.
Give only the code and key to a partner to reconstruct.
expeditions.evidence: Original picture, code and reconstructed picture.
expeditions.explanation: A digital image can represent position and color with agreed symbols; more detail may require more data.
expeditions.extension: What happens if one row is read in reverse?
expeditions.safety: Use original drawings and avoid personal information in the image.

expeditions.title: Compression Challenge
expeditions.question: Can repeated data be described more briefly?
expeditions.materials: Paper, pencil, a row of colored squares
steps: Draw a row with several repeated-color runs.
Record each run as color plus count.
Rebuild the row from your description and compare the length of both encodings.
expeditions.evidence: A coded row and an exact reconstruction check.
expeditions.explanation: Compression can exploit repetition; a particular method may save little or even add overhead on a different pattern.
expeditions.extension: Which row would be a poor match for this method?
expeditions.safety: Use invented data, not private messages.

expeditions.title: Error-Checking Messages
expeditions.question: How could a receiver notice a damaged message?
steps: Write five single-digit numbers and their sum on a message card.
A partner changes one number while leaving the sum unchanged.
Recalculate the sum, detect the mismatch and discuss what is still unknown.
expeditions.evidence: An original message, changed message and comparison.
expeditions.explanation: A checksum can reveal some errors without identifying the original data; some multiple changes can cancel out.
expeditions.extension: Can you invent two changes that preserve the sum?
expeditions.safety: This is a toy error check, not a method for securing real accounts.

expeditions.title: Packet Post
expeditions.question: Why might a digital message arrive out of order?
expeditions.materials: Paper, pencil, envelopes or folded paper
steps: Split a sentence into four numbered chunks.
Shuffle them and have a partner reconstruct the sentence.
Remove one chunk and decide how the receiver could request it.
expeditions.evidence: A packet list, reconstruction and missing-packet rule.
expeditions.explanation: Messages can be split into packets; labels help a receiver reorder them and notice gaps.
expeditions.extension: What other information would help prevent mixing two messages?
expeditions.safety: Use fictional sentences; no names, addresses or passwords.

expeditions.title: Network Detour
expeditions.question: Can a message reach its destination if a route fails?
steps: Connect four stations with several lines.
Trace a message route and count its links.
Cross out one link and find another route or explain why none exists.
expeditions.evidence: Two route drawings and a failure explanation.
expeditions.explanation: A network's connections determine possible routes; extra links can provide alternatives.
expeditions.extension: Which single link failure would be most disruptive?
expeditions.safety: This is a paper model; do not change router or device settings.

expeditions.title: Sort and Compare
expeditions.question: Which sorting strategy needs fewer comparisons?
steps: Shuffle six different numbers and sort by repeatedly finding the smallest remaining card.
Count comparisons.
Reshuffle into the same starting order and try a different strategy.
expeditions.evidence: Two methods, starting order and comparison counts.
expeditions.explanation: Efficiency depends on both the algorithm and the input; one small trial cannot prove a method always wins.
expeditions.extension: Would an already sorted list change your result?
expeditions.safety: Use large cards and keep pieces away from small children.

expeditions.title: Search a Sorted Shelf
expeditions.question: Can sorted information reduce a search?
expeditions.materials: Sixteen numbered paper cards in order
steps: Have a partner secretly choose a number.
Search by checking cards from one end and count checks.
Repeat with the same target using middle-first elimination.
expeditions.evidence: Two search paths and check counts.
expeditions.explanation: Binary search uses ordering to eliminate regions; it does not work the same way on an unsorted collection.
expeditions.extension: What happens when the target is absent?
expeditions.safety: Use pretend records rather than private household files.

expeditions.title: Sensor Decision
expeditions.question: What can a sensor tell us—and what can it miss?
steps: Invent a light sensor that reports only bright or dark.
Draw four scenes and predict its output.
Find two different scenes with the same output and discuss a better design.
expeditions.evidence: Scene-output pairs and a limitation.
expeditions.explanation: A sensor measures selected properties, not the whole situation. A single reading can have multiple explanations.
expeditions.extension: Which second measurement would help distinguish your scenes?
expeditions.safety: Use paper models; do not inspect or disable real safety sensors.

expeditions.title: Screen-Free Classifier
expeditions.question: How can examples shape a classification rule?
steps: Sort six shapes by a rule you keep secret.
Let a partner infer the rule and test it on four new shapes.
Reveal the rule and identify misleading examples.
expeditions.evidence: Training examples, predictions and test results.
expeditions.explanation: Examples can support several possible rules. Testing on unseen examples helps reveal limits; this is a simple analogy, not an AI training system.
expeditions.extension: What new example would expose a mistaken rule quickly?
expeditions.safety: Use shapes rather than judgments about people.

expeditions.title: Biased Sample Detective
expeditions.question: Can a sample give a misleading impression?
expeditions.materials: Ten paper circles in two colors, pencil
steps: Arrange most blue circles on one side and most gold on the other.
Sample only one side and predict the full color balance.
Count the whole set and compare.
expeditions.evidence: Sample prediction and full count.
expeditions.explanation: How data is selected can bias a conclusion even when every recorded observation is accurate.
expeditions.extension: How could you choose a fairer sample?
expeditions.safety: Use fictional data, not sensitive information about people.

expeditions.title: Source Trail
expeditions.question: Can we trace a claim to its original source?
expeditions.materials: Printed or adult-opened NASA page, paper
steps: Choose one factual sentence and identify the publisher and date if available.
Separate the page's observation from interpretation or prediction.
Write a source note another person could use to find it.
expeditions.evidence: One claim, source title, URL and evidence label.
expeditions.explanation: Traceable sources make checking possible; a polished appearance alone does not establish accuracy.
expeditions.extension: What would make you update this claim later?
expeditions.safety: An adult opens external links; no account, comment or personal-data submission is needed.

expeditions.title: AI Answer Audit
expeditions.question: How would we check a confident but unsupported answer?
expeditions.materials: Paper, pencil, reference book or adult-selected source
steps: Write a fictional assistant claim: all rocks float.
List what evidence could test it and compare with a trustworthy reference.
Rewrite the answer with a correction and an honest uncertainty statement.
expeditions.evidence: Original claim, verification method and corrected wording.
expeditions.explanation: Confident wording is not evidence. Generated answers need verification, especially when used to guide an activity.
expeditions.extension: Which kinds of claims need an expert rather than a quick test?
expeditions.safety: No AI account is required; do not test unsafe or medical claims.

expeditions.title: Private-by-Design Journal
expeditions.question: Which details are necessary to share a discovery?
steps: Write a fictional bird observation containing a name, exact address and time.
Remove unnecessary identifying details while retaining useful observations.
Ask a partner whether the revised note still explains the discovery.
expeditions.evidence: Before-and-after fictional notes and reasons for each removal.
expeditions.explanation: Data minimization keeps information limited to the purpose; location and timing can reveal more than expected.
expeditions.extension: What additional consent would a photograph need?
expeditions.safety: Use invented details only; do not publish a real child's location or schedule.

expeditions.title: Accessible Button Lab
expeditions.question: Can someone understand a control without color clues?
steps: Draw three buttons that differ only by color.
Redraw them with words and distinct shapes.
Ask a partner to explain their functions using a plain-pencil copy.
expeditions.evidence: Two designs and feedback from a voluntary tester.
expeditions.explanation: Redundant labels can make meaning available without relying on color alone; one test does not establish universal accessibility.
expeditions.extension: How might someone using audio encounter these controls?
expeditions.safety: Ask permission before testing; accept different reading and communication needs.

expeditions.title: Offline Expedition Kit
expeditions.question: What should still work without an internet connection?
steps: List everything needed to carry out the activity.
Mark which parts currently require a screen or link.
Prepare a paper instruction sheet and have a partner try following it.
expeditions.evidence: A dependency list and revised offline sheet.
expeditions.explanation: Designing for limited connectivity makes hidden dependencies visible.
expeditions.extension: Which reference information should be included rather than merely linked?
expeditions.safety: Keep safety instructions on the paper copy; do not remove them to save space.

expeditions.title: Version Detective
expeditions.question: How can we tell which instruction changed?
expeditions.materials: Two paper copies of a short invented procedure
steps: Write version one and test it with a partner.
Change one confusing step, label version two and date both.
Compare the copies and explain why the revision helps.
expeditions.evidence: Two dated versions and a short change note.
expeditions.explanation: Version history preserves the reason for a change and makes comparison possible.
expeditions.extension: What would you need to safely restore the earlier version?
expeditions.safety: Use a harmless paper-folding procedure, not equipment instructions.

expeditions.title: Human-in-the-Loop
expeditions.question: When should a system stop and ask for help?
steps: Invent a rule that sorts parcels by labeled size.
Add a parcel with a missing label and one with conflicting labels.
Design a stop-and-ask response and test all examples.
expeditions.evidence: A decision chart including uncertain cases.
expeditions.explanation: A system can be designed to acknowledge insufficient information rather than guess.
expeditions.extension: What should the system show the person asked to help?
expeditions.safety: Use pretend parcels; no real deliveries, addresses or account data.

expeditions.title: Interface Paper Prototype
expeditions.question: Can a family find an expedition without instructions?
expeditions.materials: Paper, pencil, three drawn screen layouts
steps: Draw a home screen, category screen and activity screen.
Ask a willing partner to find a chosen activity while you swap pages.
Record confusion and revise one navigation label.
expeditions.evidence: Screen sketches, observations and a revision.
expeditions.explanation: A paper prototype can reveal navigation problems before code is written.
expeditions.extension: Could the tester return to the category from every screen?
expeditions.safety: Do not record a tester's name or voice; participation is optional.

expeditions.title: Technology Failure Plan
expeditions.question: What happens when a useful tool becomes unavailable?
expeditions.materials: Notebook, pencil, a familiar learning task
steps: Choose a task such as identifying a sky pattern.
List what you would do if power, connectivity or the app failed.
Test one fallback using a paper guide or direct observation.
expeditions.evidence: A fallback plan and a record of its test.
expeditions.explanation: Resilient designs make important tasks possible despite individual failures.
expeditions.extension: Which fallback preserves evidence rather than encouraging a guess?
expeditions.safety: Use a learning task, never simulate failures in emergency or safety equipment.

expeditions.title: Paper Bridge
expeditions.question: Which fold helps paper span a gap?
expeditions.materials: Two books, paper, ruler, large identical blocks
steps: Set books ten centimeters apart and bridge them with a flat sheet.
Add blocks one at a time until the paper sags; stop before anything falls.
Repeat using an accordion-folded sheet with the same span and paper size.
expeditions.evidence: Two designs and their supported block counts.
expeditions.explanation: Shape changes how a structure carries a load; a fair comparison keeps material and span similar.
expeditions.extension: Can you improve the bridge with the same sheet?
expeditions.safety: Build on the floor with lightweight blocks; never stand on a model.

expeditions.title: Tower Footprint
expeditions.question: How does base width affect a paper tower?
steps: Build two equally tall rolled-paper towers with different base widths.
Place each on the same base and tilt it very gently.
Compare the first visible lean and redesign one tower.
expeditions.evidence: Measured heights, base widths and stability notes.
expeditions.explanation: Stability depends on the relationship between support area and mass distribution.
expeditions.extension: Can you improve stability without adding material?
expeditions.safety: Use lightweight paper models on the floor; keep clear of faces.

expeditions.title: Cargo Boat
expeditions.question: Can the same foil carry different loads after reshaping?
expeditions.materials: Foil, shallow tray of water, large identical blocks
steps: Form a boat from one foil square and add blocks slowly.
Record the load before water enters.
Dry and reshape the same foil, then repeat with the same blocks.
expeditions.evidence: Two hull sketches and load counts.
expeditions.explanation: Hull shape affects displaced water and stability; leaks can invalidate a comparison.
expeditions.extension: What tradeoff appears between a wide hull and high sides?
expeditions.safety: Adult supervises water and chooses large blocks; no sharp foil edges or small weights.

expeditions.title: Rolling Delivery
expeditions.question: How can a ramp deliver a toy accurately?
expeditions.materials: Cardboard, books, large toy car, paper target
steps: Build a low ramp aimed at a floor target.
Release from the same position three times and measure the miss distance.
Change one ramp feature and repeat.
expeditions.evidence: Six landing positions and one design change.
expeditions.explanation: Engineering tests compare performance against a stated goal; repeatability matters as well as one success.
expeditions.extension: Can you improve accuracy while using fewer supports?
expeditions.safety: Keep ramps low and the floor route clear.

expeditions.title: Paper Landing Pad
expeditions.question: Which structure cushions a soft cargo's short fall?
expeditions.materials: Paper, tape, small soft toy, tray
steps: Make a flat pad and a folded pad with equal paper amounts.
An adult releases the soft toy from the same low height above each.
Compare bounce and displacement, then revise one pad.
expeditions.evidence: Pad sketches and repeated bounce descriptions.
expeditions.explanation: Deforming structures can change how a landing happens; this model does not certify protective equipment.
expeditions.extension: How could you make the comparison more measurable?
expeditions.safety: Use only soft cargo below knee height; no eggs, glass or people as test loads.

expeditions.title: Shade Shelter Model
expeditions.question: Can a small roof shade a paper figure from different angles?
expeditions.materials: Card, tape, LED flashlight, paper figure
steps: Build a freestanding shelter for the figure.
Shine the flashlight from three marked positions and draw shaded areas.
Adjust the roof while keeping the material budget fixed.
expeditions.evidence: Three light tests and a revised roof.
expeditions.explanation: A design that works for one direction may fail under another condition.
expeditions.extension: Could the figure still enter the shelter easily?
expeditions.safety: Use an LED flashlight, not sunlight or hot lamps; adults handle cutting.

expeditions.title: Rain Roof Model
expeditions.question: Which roof shape sheds a small amount of water?
expeditions.materials: Cardboard, foil, tape, tray, spoon, water
steps: Cover two roof shapes with equal foil amounts.
Drip equal spoonfuls of water onto each over a tray.
Record pooling and leaks, then adjust one joint.
expeditions.evidence: Roof drawings, water amounts and leak notes.
expeditions.explanation: Shape and joints both influence water pathways; a model test is limited to the conditions used.
expeditions.extension: How would wind-driven rain challenge your design?
expeditions.safety: Use small water amounts away from electronics; wipe spills and recycle dry materials.

expeditions.title: Wind-Stable Sign
expeditions.question: How can a model sign resist a gentle breeze?
expeditions.materials: Paper, card, tape, handheld paper fan
steps: Build a small standing sign with a readable message.
Fan it gently from a marked distance for five strokes.
Change its support and repeat without changing the fan routine.
expeditions.evidence: Before-and-after support sketches and movement notes.
expeditions.explanation: Supports must balance stability, visibility and material use; hand fanning is an approximate test.
expeditions.extension: Could a lower sign perform better with less material?
expeditions.safety: Use a paper fan rather than electrical fans; keep the model on a table away from edges.

expeditions.title: Paper Beam Shapes
expeditions.question: Which cross-section resists bending?
expeditions.materials: Equal paper sheets, tape, two supports, large blocks
steps: Form a flat strip, a folded channel and a tube from equal sheets.
Bridge the same gap with each and add lightweight blocks.
Compare bending at the same load.
expeditions.evidence: Three cross-sections and bending observations.
expeditions.explanation: Material arrangement changes structural behavior even when the material amount stays similar.
expeditions.extension: Would rotating a channel change its performance?
expeditions.safety: Build near floor level with lightweight objects; stop before collapse.

expeditions.title: Cardboard Gusset
expeditions.question: Can a corner brace stiffen a frame?
expeditions.materials: Card strips, tape, adult-prepared triangular pieces
steps: Tape four strips into a rectangle and gently push sideways.
Add triangular corner braces without changing the frame size.
Repeat the gentle push and compare deformation.
expeditions.evidence: Two frame sketches and qualitative deformation notes.
expeditions.explanation: Bracing can restrict shape changes; hand-applied force is not a precise load measurement.
expeditions.extension: Where could one brace help most?
expeditions.safety: Adults prepare pieces; use gentle pushes and no sharp tools.

expeditions.title: Paper Hinge
expeditions.question: Which folded hinge survives repeated opening?
steps: Make a paper hinge joining two card panels.
Open and close it twenty times using the same range.
Redesign the fold or tape placement and repeat.
expeditions.evidence: Cycle counts, damage notes and two designs.
expeditions.explanation: Durability is a performance requirement that can be tested through repeated use.
expeditions.extension: What would a fair comparison between materials require?
expeditions.safety: Use smooth paper edges; keep fingers clear of any stiff pinch points.

expeditions.title: Rover Wheel Tradeoffs
expeditions.question: What wheel properties would help a model cross rough ground?
expeditions.materials: Card, pencil, toy vehicle if available, folded-paper terrain
steps: Draw two wheel designs for a small rover and state a goal.
Roll an available toy gently over smooth and folded-paper paths; if unavailable, trace a paper model and label it untested.
Revise the design using observed evidence and name what still needs testing.
expeditions.evidence: A wheel proposal with tested and untested claims separated.
expeditions.explanation: A design proposal is not a proven mechanism; terrain, grip and wheel size interact.
expeditions.extension: What prototype would test your biggest uncertainty?
expeditions.safety: Use dry tabletop materials and large toys; do not modify electrical vehicles.

expeditions.title: Accessible Ramp Model
expeditions.question: Can a gentler route fit a limited space?
steps: Create two ramps reaching the same small height with different lengths.
Compare their slopes and the space each occupies.
Draw a route that includes a landing within a marked tabletop area.
expeditions.evidence: Dimensions and a plan showing space tradeoffs.
expeditions.explanation: A gentler slope generally takes more horizontal space; this model is not a building-code specification.
expeditions.extension: How could a turn change the space needed?
expeditions.safety: Tabletop models only; do not construct ramps for people or mobility devices.

expeditions.title: Drainage Landscape
expeditions.question: How does a channel guide water around a model building?
expeditions.materials: Foil tray, reusable modeling clay, spoon, water
steps: Shape a small landscape with a raised building zone.
Add three spoonfuls of water at a marked point and observe its route.
Add a channel and repeat with the same water amount.
expeditions.evidence: Two maps of water paths.
expeditions.explanation: Slope and barriers redirect flow; a tabletop model omits many real drainage conditions.
expeditions.extension: Where might water collect after your change?
expeditions.safety: Adult supervision; small water amounts only, no outdoor drainage changes.

expeditions.title: Sorting Screen
expeditions.question: Can opening size separate different paper shapes?
expeditions.materials: Cardboard with adult-made openings, large paper pieces, tray
steps: Choose large paper pieces in two sizes and predict which will pass.
Test each through the screen without forcing it.
Redesign one opening and compare results.
expeditions.evidence: Opening measurements and a pass-or-stop table.
expeditions.explanation: A screen selects by physical dimensions; orientation can affect whether something passes.
expeditions.extension: How would flexible pieces complicate the design?
expeditions.safety: Adults cut openings; use paper rather than sand, food or tiny beads.

expeditions.title: Clean Water Model
expeditions.question: Can removing visible particles prove water is drinkable?
expeditions.materials: Clear cup, water, large clean paper scraps, colander, tray
steps: Add clean paper scraps to water and describe the mixture.
Pour through a colander over a tray with adult help.
Compare visible particles before and after and state what the test cannot detect.
expeditions.evidence: A separation record and an explicit not-safe-to-drink conclusion.
expeditions.explanation: Removing visible pieces does not establish removal of microbes or dissolved substances.
expeditions.extension: What information would a water-safety expert need beyond appearance?
expeditions.safety: Do not drink any water used here. This is a separation model, not a drinking-water treatment method.

expeditions.title: Gripper Prototype
expeditions.question: Can folded paper move a soft object without fingers touching it?
steps: Fold a card into a springy gripper.
Move the ball between two marked spots five times and count drops.
Change the contact shape and retest.
expeditions.evidence: Two grippers and success counts out of five.
expeditions.explanation: Contact area and grip geometry influence control; improvement depends on the chosen task.
expeditions.extension: Can your gripper handle a larger soft object?
expeditions.safety: Use paper cargo only; do not grip people, pets or fragile objects.

expeditions.title: Packaging Corners
expeditions.question: Which package keeps a paper model in place?
expeditions.materials: Small box, scrap paper, lightweight card model
steps: Pack the model using a fixed amount of paper.
An adult gently tips the closed box in four directions.
Inspect movement, then redesign supports and retest.
expeditions.evidence: Packing diagrams and movement notes.
expeditions.explanation: Packaging can restrain movement as well as cushion impacts; this test evaluates only gentle tipping.
expeditions.extension: How could you use less material without losing restraint?
expeditions.safety: No dropping, glass, liquids or live objects; use a small lightweight box.

expeditions.title: Sound Barrier Model
expeditions.question: Can a barrier change how a quiet sound is heard?
expeditions.materials: Cardboard panel, folded towel, quiet tapping source
steps: Listen from one fixed place while a partner taps gently.
Place cardboard between source and listener, then compare with a towel in the same position.
Repeat and note disagreements rather than forcing a winner.
expeditions.evidence: Repeated listening descriptions and setup sketch.
expeditions.explanation: Sound can travel around and through barriers; a subjective listening test has limits.
expeditions.extension: How could you measure changes more consistently?
expeditions.safety: Keep sounds soft and comfortable; never block ears with objects.

expeditions.title: Light Shield Design
expeditions.question: Can a shade direct useful light away from eyes?
steps: Aim the flashlight at a tabletop target.
Build a loose paper shade around the front without covering switches or vents.
Compare target illumination and spill from the same viewing position.
expeditions.evidence: Two sketches showing target and spill light.
expeditions.explanation: A shield changes where light reaches; reducing glare may also reduce useful illumination.
expeditions.extension: What shape balances both goals?
expeditions.safety: Use a cool LED flashlight briefly, no hot lamps, and keep beams away from eyes.

expeditions.title: Book Stand
expeditions.question: Can a small stand hold a light notebook open?
steps: Sketch a stand and state the viewing angle you want.
Build it and test with a light notebook on a low table.
Adjust one support and compare stability and readability.
expeditions.evidence: Design dimensions and two test notes.
expeditions.explanation: A design must meet several requirements at once; more tilt may affect stability.
expeditions.extension: Could the stand fold flat for storage?
expeditions.safety: Adults cut card; use a light notebook and never a heavy device.

expeditions.title: Reusable Fastener
expeditions.question: Can a paper connection be opened and closed repeatedly?
steps: Design a tab-and-slot connection without adhesive at the joint.
Open and close it ten times and inspect damage.
Revise tab width and compare another ten cycles.
expeditions.evidence: Two dimensions and cycle-by-cycle wear notes.
expeditions.explanation: A connection trades holding strength against ease of release and wear.
expeditions.extension: What failure would tell you the joint needs replacing?
expeditions.safety: Adults cut slots; use smooth card and gentle force.

expeditions.title: Desk Organizer
expeditions.question: Can an organizer fit supplies and remain easy to use?
expeditions.materials: Reused small boxes, paper, tape, ruler
steps: Measure three safe desk items and sketch compartments.
Build within a marked footprint.
Ask a partner to retrieve each item and revise a difficult compartment.
expeditions.evidence: Measurements, layout and tester feedback.
expeditions.explanation: Design for use includes reach and visibility, not just fitting objects into space.
expeditions.extension: How would a left-handed user change your layout?
expeditions.safety: Use lightweight items with no sharp points and clean boxes.

expeditions.title: Repair Before Replace
expeditions.question: Can we restore a torn paper structure thoughtfully?
expeditions.materials: Torn paper folder, tape, scrap paper
steps: Describe how the folder failed and what it must do.
Compare two patch sketches, then apply one.
Test with a few sheets and record whether the tear spreads.
expeditions.evidence: Failure description, repair choice and test evidence.
expeditions.explanation: Repair begins with understanding failure; extra material helps only if placed usefully.
expeditions.extension: How could a new design prevent the same failure?
expeditions.safety: Repair paper only; never attempt electrical, protective or load-bearing equipment repairs.

expeditions.title: Constraint Challenge
expeditions.question: Which design best meets two competing goals?
expeditions.materials: Paper, tape, ruler, large lightweight block
steps: Build a paper platform at least five centimeters high using one sheet.
Test whether it supports one block for ten seconds and record material used.
Revise for less tape while keeping the same support goal.
expeditions.evidence: Two designs scored against explicit requirements.
expeditions.explanation: Engineering choices involve tradeoffs; a design is successful relative to stated criteria and constraints.
expeditions.extension: What new requirement would change your preferred design?
expeditions.safety: Use a lightweight block and floor-level testing; no human loads.

expeditions.title: Observation Sketchbook
expeditions.question: What changes when we draw from observation instead of memory?
steps: Draw the object from memory for two minutes.
Place it in view and make a second drawing with labels for details.
Compare what you noticed rather than judging which drawing is prettier.
expeditions.evidence: Two drawings and three newly noticed details.
expeditions.explanation: Drawing can make attention visible; observation and interpretation both influence an image.
expeditions.extension: Which detail would you investigate more closely?
expeditions.safety: Choose a safe object and work in comfortable lighting.

expeditions.title: Lines With Purpose
expeditions.question: How can line choices suggest movement?
steps: Draw the same imagined breeze using straight, curved and broken lines.
Ask a partner what motion each suggests.
Revise one drawing to communicate a specific direction.
expeditions.evidence: Three line studies and feedback.
expeditions.explanation: Lines can communicate movement, but viewers may interpret the same marks differently.
expeditions.extension: How could a label help without replacing the image?
expeditions.safety: Partner feedback is optional; accept different interpretations.

expeditions.title: Texture Library
expeditions.question: Can marks communicate how a surface looks or feels?
steps: Observe three textures without rubbing fragile objects.
Invent pencil marks for each texture.
Ask a partner to match drawings to surfaces and explain their choices.
expeditions.evidence: Three texture studies and matching notes.
expeditions.explanation: Artists can suggest texture through marks without using the original material.
expeditions.extension: Could you represent the same texture at two scales?
expeditions.safety: No rubbing monuments, living plants or fragile surfaces; avoid unknown materials.

expeditions.title: Negative Space
expeditions.question: Can drawing the space around an object reveal its shape?
expeditions.materials: Paper, pencil, chair or large household object
steps: Sketch the empty spaces around and within the object.
Add the object's outer boundary afterward.
Compare with a direct outline sketch.
expeditions.evidence: Two approaches and a note about what became easier.
expeditions.explanation: Negative space is the area around or between forms; attending to it offers another way to observe proportions.
expeditions.extension: Which object would have especially interesting gaps?
expeditions.safety: Observe from a stable seated position; no climbing to find a view.

expeditions.title: Value Ladder
expeditions.question: How can light and dark suggest form without color?
steps: Make five patches from light to dark using pencil pressure or hatching.
Sketch the cup and use the patches to suggest light and shadow.
Label the direction of the room light.
expeditions.evidence: A value scale and shaded sketch.
expeditions.explanation: Value describes lightness and darkness; shading is a representation of observed illumination.
expeditions.extension: How would the sketch change if the light moved?
expeditions.safety: Use normal room lighting; never stare at bright sources.

expeditions.title: Color Mood Study
expeditions.question: How do color choices change a viewer's impression?
steps: Draw the same simple landscape twice.
Use different color groups while keeping shapes alike.
Invite a partner to describe each and note where their response differs from yours.
expeditions.evidence: Two studies and a comparison of interpretations.
expeditions.explanation: Color associations can vary by person and context; an intended mood is not a universal rule.
expeditions.extension: Could a title change how viewers read the colors?
expeditions.safety: Do not label one emotional response as correct.

expeditions.title: Composition Frames
expeditions.question: How does cropping change a story?
expeditions.materials: Paper, pencil, two paper frame corners
steps: Sketch a safe room scene.
Use paper corners to frame two different parts of the drawing.
Explain what each frame emphasizes or leaves out.
expeditions.evidence: Two crops and a written explanation.
expeditions.explanation: Composition directs attention through choices about inclusion, placement and emphasis.
expeditions.extension: What important context disappears in the tightest crop?
expeditions.safety: Do not photograph people or private documents without permission.

expeditions.title: Scale for Storytelling
expeditions.question: How can size in an image communicate importance?
steps: Draw a garden scene with ordinary relative sizes.
Make a second version exaggerating one feature.
Label the second as imaginative and explain the storytelling effect.
expeditions.evidence: Observed-proportion and imaginative versions.
expeditions.explanation: Artistic scale can serve expression; scientific illustrations need clear labels when scale is altered.
expeditions.extension: When would exaggerated scale mislead a learner?
expeditions.safety: Distinguish invention from measurement in captions.

expeditions.title: Scientific Caption Studio
expeditions.question: What should a caption tell an explorer?
expeditions.materials: An ELS illustration or your own sketch, paper
steps: Write a caption naming what the image represents.
Add whether it is a photograph, model or imagined scene and whether it is to scale.
Ask a partner what uncertainty remains.
expeditions.evidence: Original and revised captions.
expeditions.explanation: A caption can clarify provenance and limits that an image alone cannot communicate.
expeditions.extension: What source credit belongs beside the image?
expeditions.safety: Use your own work or linked public reference pages; do not assume every online image is reusable.

expeditions.title: Data to Sound on Paper
expeditions.question: Can a sound pattern represent data without pretending to be a recording?
expeditions.materials: Paper, pencil, five invented temperature values
steps: Map low, middle and high values to three gentle tap patterns.
Write a score for the five values and perform it softly.
Ask a partner to decode with your key.
expeditions.evidence: Values, mapping key and decoded result.
expeditions.explanation: Sonification assigns sound to data; the chosen mapping is a design decision, not the original object's sound.
expeditions.extension: Would a different mapping reveal another pattern?
expeditions.safety: Keep sounds soft; offer a silent visual score instead.

expeditions.title: Rhythm Fractions
expeditions.question: How can a rhythm fill the same amount of time in different ways?
steps: Draw a four-beat bar and clap four even beats gently.
Replace pairs of beats with longer holds or rests while keeping the bar length.
Write and perform two patterns for a partner.
expeditions.evidence: Two notated patterns and a count check.
expeditions.explanation: Rhythmic notation organizes duration; different patterns can share the same total time.
expeditions.extension: Can you write a pattern with more rests than sounds?
expeditions.safety: Keep volume comfortable; pointing to beats is an equal alternative to clapping.

expeditions.title: Found Sound Map
expeditions.question: What does a place sound like without recording it?
steps: Listen for two minutes from one safe spot.
Draw symbols for sounds and approximate directions without naming people.
Repeat later and compare what changed.
expeditions.evidence: Two sound maps with times and a symbol key.
expeditions.explanation: A sound map represents a listener's experience; attention and position influence the record.
expeditions.extension: Which sounds might another listener notice first?
expeditions.safety: No audio recording required; avoid private conversations and use visual observation if preferred.

expeditions.title: Four-Panel Discovery
expeditions.question: Can a short comic explain a change in thinking?
steps: Choose an observation from another expedition.
Draw four panels: question, prediction, evidence and revised explanation.
Ask a reader to identify where your thinking changed.
expeditions.evidence: A four-panel comic and reader feedback.
expeditions.explanation: Sequential images can show reasoning as a process rather than presenting only a final answer.
expeditions.extension: Where should an uncertainty appear in the story?
expeditions.safety: Use fictional characters or ask consent before depicting identifiable people.

expeditions.title: Storyboard a Field Visit
expeditions.question: How can a storyboard prepare a safe exploration?
steps: Draw six panels for a hypothetical park observation with an adult.
Include preparation, observation, recording and return.
Add a weather-change panel and revise the sequence.
expeditions.evidence: A six-panel plan with a fallback.
expeditions.explanation: Storyboards make sequence and missing steps visible before an event occurs.
expeditions.extension: What could be done from a window instead?
expeditions.safety: This is a plan, not permission to travel; an adult chooses routes and conditions.

expeditions.title: Museum Label
expeditions.question: How can a short label invite curiosity without overstating facts?
steps: Write a title and two observed facts about the object.
Add one open question and mark any uncertain history.
Ask a reader what they would inspect next.
expeditions.evidence: A concise label with fact and question separated.
expeditions.explanation: Interpretive labels select useful context; acknowledging unknowns can invite investigation.
expeditions.extension: What source would help verify the object's history?
expeditions.safety: Do not display private family information or valuable objects publicly.

expeditions.title: Pattern From Nature
expeditions.question: How can an observed pattern inspire an original design?
expeditions.materials: Leaf sketch or safe view, paper, pencils
steps: Observe a repeating shape without collecting living material.
Simplify it into a motif and repeat it across a border.
Label which features were observed and which you invented.
expeditions.evidence: Observation sketch, motif and border.
expeditions.explanation: Design can transform observations while keeping the origin of the idea clear.
expeditions.extension: How would rotating the motif change the pattern?
expeditions.safety: Avoid copying sacred or culturally restricted motifs; use your own observations.

expeditions.title: Symmetry and Surprise
expeditions.question: What changes when a symmetric design has one deliberate difference?
steps: Fold paper lightly to mark a center line and draw mirrored shapes.
Make a second version with one intentional asymmetry.
Ask a partner where their attention goes first.
expeditions.evidence: Two designs and attention notes.
expeditions.explanation: Symmetry and contrast can shape visual attention, but responses vary.
expeditions.extension: Can you create balance without mirror symmetry?
expeditions.safety: Use age-appropriate materials and avoid perfection-based scoring.

expeditions.title: Perspective Window
expeditions.question: Why do distant objects often look smaller in a drawing?
steps: Sketch two similar objects at different distances.
Mark where their tops and bottoms appear in your view.
Explain why apparent size alone does not reveal actual size.
expeditions.evidence: A labeled view and a distinction between actual and apparent size.
expeditions.explanation: Perspective represents spatial relationships from a particular viewpoint.
expeditions.extension: What other clue could help compare the objects' true sizes?
expeditions.safety: Observe while stationary; do not stand in roads or on furniture.

expeditions.title: Accessible Poster
expeditions.question: Can a poster communicate without relying on color alone?
steps: Design a poster inviting a family to a fictional observation activity.
Add a clear title, readable contrast and text labels for symbols.
Ask a partner to find the time, purpose and materials, then revise.
expeditions.evidence: Two poster versions and three findability notes.
expeditions.explanation: Communication design includes readability and information hierarchy; one reader's feedback is a starting point.
expeditions.extension: Would the message survive a plain black-and-white copy?
expeditions.safety: Use fictional contact details and no real child's photograph.

expeditions.title: Audio Description Draft
expeditions.question: How can words convey an image's important information?
steps: Write a short description naming the subject and arrangement.
Read it to a partner who has not seen the drawing.
Compare their understanding with your intent and revise without calling it a perfect substitute.
expeditions.evidence: Two descriptions and feedback.
expeditions.explanation: Useful descriptions depend on purpose; describing every detail can hide the central information.
expeditions.extension: What would change for a scientific diagram rather than a landscape?
expeditions.safety: Do not blindfold anyone; participation is voluntary and can be entirely written.

expeditions.title: Observation Poetry
expeditions.question: Can a poem preserve evidence while expressing wonder?
steps: List five things you can directly observe.
Write a short poem using three observations and one clearly imaginative comparison.
Underline the observed details and label the comparison.
expeditions.evidence: A poem with evidence and imagination distinguished.
expeditions.explanation: Creative language and factual observation can coexist when readers can tell their roles apart.
expeditions.extension: Which line invites a new question?
expeditions.safety: Observe from a safe place and avoid identifying strangers.

expeditions.title: Mini Exhibition
expeditions.question: How does arranging work affect a visitor's understanding?
steps: Choose three expedition drawings and decide an order.
Write a short label for each and a question for the whole display.
Invite a willing viewer to describe the story and revise the order.
expeditions.evidence: An exhibition plan and visitor feedback.
expeditions.explanation: Curation builds relationships among works through selection, sequence and context.
expeditions.extension: Would chronological order tell a different story?
expeditions.safety: Use your own work or obtain permission; display no private information.

expeditions.title: Credit the Creator
expeditions.question: What information helps us acknowledge creative work fairly?
steps: Write a credit naming the creator, title and date.
Add whether another reference inspired it and identify that reference.
Compare attribution with permission: explain why credit alone does not grant reuse rights.
expeditions.evidence: A credit line and a reuse-question checklist.
expeditions.explanation: Provenance explains where work came from; attribution and permission answer different questions.
expeditions.extension: What would you ask before adapting someone else's work?
expeditions.safety: Do not upload or reuse another person's work without appropriate permission.

expeditions.title: Motion Flipbook
expeditions.question: How can still images suggest motion?
steps: Draw a ball in slightly different positions on eight pages.
Flip the pages and compare even and uneven spacing.
Revise the sequence to suggest slowing down.
expeditions.evidence: Two sequences and a note about spacing.
expeditions.explanation: A sequence of changing images can suggest motion; spacing and display timing affect the impression.
expeditions.extension: Can you communicate motion with just four frames?
expeditions.safety: Flip gently; no flashing lights or rapid full-screen effects are needed.

expeditions.title: Design a Discovery Symbol
expeditions.question: Can an original symbol communicate an activity clearly?
steps: Choose an activity such as observing or measuring and sketch three symbols.
Ask a partner what each means before explaining.
Refine one and pair it with a text label.
expeditions.evidence: Three concepts, feedback and final labeled symbol.
expeditions.explanation: Symbols depend on shared interpretation; accompanying words can reduce ambiguity.
expeditions.extension: How would you test it with someone new to ELS?
expeditions.safety: This is an explorer exercise, not a replacement for official ELS branding.

expeditions.title: Estimate Then Measure
expeditions.question: How close can an estimate be without pretending it is exact?
expeditions.materials: Ruler, paper, pencil, three safe objects
steps: Estimate each object's length and write units before measuring.
Measure from the ruler's zero mark.
Calculate the difference between estimate and measurement and explain one revision.
expeditions.evidence: Three estimates, measurements and differences.
expeditions.explanation: An estimate and a measurement serve different purposes; both should name units and reasonable precision.
expeditions.extension: Which object was hardest to estimate, and why?
expeditions.safety: Choose accessible tabletop objects; no climbing to measure.

expeditions.title: Unit Detective
expeditions.question: Why can two correct measurements have different numbers?
expeditions.materials: Ruler with centimeters and inches, paper
steps: Measure one object in centimeters and inches.
Record the units beside every number.
Explain why the numerical values differ without the object changing.
expeditions.evidence: Two measurements of each of three objects.
expeditions.explanation: A measurement combines a number and a unit; comparing bare numbers can mislead.
expeditions.extension: What happens if someone omits the unit?
expeditions.safety: Use a safe ruler and ordinary objects.

expeditions.title: Perimeter Walk on Paper
expeditions.question: Can shapes with equal perimeters enclose different areas?
steps: Draw rectangles with side lengths 1 by 5 and 2 by 4 grid units.
Count each perimeter and area.
Find another rectangle with the same perimeter and compare its area.
expeditions.evidence: Drawings with labeled perimeter and area.
expeditions.explanation: Perimeter measures boundary length; area measures covered surface. Equal perimeters need not mean equal areas.
expeditions.extension: Which whole-number rectangle maximizes area for this perimeter?
expeditions.safety: Use drawings rather than marking public or private ground.

expeditions.title: Area Tile Lab
expeditions.question: How can we measure area with repeated units?
steps: Cover a rectangular card with equal squares without gaps or overlap.
Count rows and columns and multiply.
Compare your multiplication with the total tile count.
expeditions.evidence: A tiled drawing and two matching calculations.
expeditions.explanation: Area units must cover consistently; rows and columns provide an efficient counting structure.
expeditions.extension: What would you do with a partial square at the edge?
expeditions.safety: Use large paper squares and adult-prepared materials.

expeditions.title: Fraction Fold
expeditions.question: Can different folds name the same amount?
steps: Fold one sheet into halves and another equal sheet into quarters.
Shade one half and two quarters.
Align the sheets and explain the relationship.
expeditions.evidence: Two shaded models and an equivalence statement.
expeditions.explanation: Equivalent fractions describe the same proportion when the wholes are the same size.
expeditions.extension: What changes if the sheets have different sizes?
expeditions.safety: Fold only; cutting is unnecessary.

expeditions.title: Ratio Color Recipe
expeditions.question: How can we enlarge a pattern without changing its ratio?
steps: Make a pattern with two blue squares for every three gold squares.
Double and triple both counts.
Compare the ratios and explain why adding one to each count is different.
expeditions.evidence: Three scaled recipes and one counterexample.
expeditions.explanation: Multiplying both parts by the same factor preserves a ratio; adding equal amounts generally does not.
expeditions.extension: Can a pattern of twenty squares use this ratio exactly?
expeditions.safety: Use pencil marks rather than food or small beads.

expeditions.title: Scale Map
expeditions.question: How can a small drawing represent a larger space?
expeditions.materials: Paper, ruler, measurements of a safe tabletop
steps: Measure a tabletop's length and width.
Choose a scale such as one drawing centimeter for ten real centimeters.
Draw its boundary and verify both dimensions using the same scale.
expeditions.evidence: A map with scale, units and checked dimensions.
expeditions.explanation: A scale drawing uses a consistent relationship between represented and actual lengths.
expeditions.extension: What details become too small to draw clearly?
expeditions.safety: Measure only reachable surfaces and omit private room details from shared work.

expeditions.title: Coordinate Treasure
expeditions.question: How can two numbers locate a point?
steps: Draw and label horizontal and vertical axes from zero to five.
Place three imaginary treasures and write coordinates in horizontal-then-vertical order.
Have a partner plot them from the list.
expeditions.evidence: A coordinate list and matching map.
expeditions.explanation: An ordered pair identifies position relative to agreed axes; reversing the order can change the location.
expeditions.extension: Which points stay in the same place when their coordinates are reversed?
expeditions.safety: Use an imaginary map, not real personal locations.

expeditions.title: Route Choices
expeditions.question: Is the shortest-looking route always shortest on a grid?
steps: Mark a start, finish and two blocked squares.
Draw three legal routes using horizontal and vertical moves only.
Count moves and compare routes under the same rules.
expeditions.evidence: Three routes with move counts.
expeditions.explanation: An optimization problem needs explicit rules; diagonal shortcuts change the problem.
expeditions.extension: Can you justify that no shorter legal route exists?
expeditions.safety: Paper puzzle only; do not use it as real travel guidance.

expeditions.title: Symmetry Search
expeditions.question: Which shapes match themselves after a reflection?
steps: Predict mirror lines for a square, rectangle and irregular shape.
Fold or trace to test each proposed line.
Record a prediction that failed and why.
expeditions.evidence: Shapes with tested symmetry lines.
expeditions.explanation: Reflection symmetry requires corresponding parts to coincide, not merely look approximately balanced.
expeditions.extension: How many mirror lines does an equilateral triangle have?
expeditions.safety: Use paper folds and no glass mirrors.

expeditions.title: Angle Turns
expeditions.question: How can a turn be described without a compass direction?
steps: Draw a starting arrow and make a quarter turn.
Combine four quarter turns and compare with the start.
Create a route using half and quarter turns for a partner.
expeditions.evidence: A turn sequence and final direction.
expeditions.explanation: A full turn is 360 degrees; a quarter turn is 90 and a half turn is 180.
expeditions.extension: Does changing the order of turns and moves change a route?
expeditions.safety: Move paper arrows on a table rather than walking with closed eyes.

expeditions.title: Pattern Rule Lab
expeditions.question: Can more than one rule fit a short sequence?
steps: Write 2, 4, 6 and predict the next number.
Invent a different rule that fits the first three terms but continues differently.
Explain why more evidence or a stated rule is needed.
expeditions.evidence: Two valid continuations with rules.
expeditions.explanation: A short pattern can support multiple rules; a plausible continuation is not uniquely proven.
expeditions.extension: What extra information would settle the intended rule?
expeditions.safety: Use invented number patterns; no safety considerations beyond ordinary stationery.

expeditions.title: Function Machine
expeditions.question: Can inputs reveal an unknown rule?
steps: A partner chooses a rule such as multiply by two then add one.
Give four inputs and record outputs.
Propose a rule and test it on a new input before revealing the original.
expeditions.evidence: An input-output table and a test prediction.
expeditions.explanation: Testing a rule on a new case checks a prediction, though finitely many examples may still allow other rules.
expeditions.extension: Which input would be most useful to ask for next?
expeditions.safety: Use small whole numbers and allow drawing or counters on paper.

expeditions.title: Fair Sharing
expeditions.question: How can we share a quantity equally when it does not divide neatly?
steps: Draw thirteen supplies for four imaginary teams.
Share equal whole units and record what remains.
Discuss whether dividing a supply is allowed, then express the result under each rule.
expeditions.evidence: Whole-unit allocation and optional fractional allocation.
expeditions.explanation: Division depends on the meaning of the objects; some quantities can be split and some cannot.
expeditions.extension: How does the answer change for thirteen meters of ribbon?
expeditions.safety: Use drawings rather than food; no cutting needed.

expeditions.title: Probability Bag on Paper
expeditions.question: Does a likely outcome have to happen next?
expeditions.materials: Six folded paper cards, bowl, pencil
steps: Label four cards blue and two gold; mix them.
Draw one, record it, replace it and remix, twenty times.
Compare the tally with your prediction without expecting an exact match.
expeditions.evidence: Twenty results and relative frequencies.
expeditions.explanation: Probability describes uncertainty; a small sample can differ from the long-run proportion.
expeditions.extension: What would removing cards without replacement change?
expeditions.safety: Use large folded cards and keep materials away from very young children.

expeditions.title: Sample Size
expeditions.question: How stable is an estimate after more observations?
steps: Flip a paper card ten times and record which side lands up.
Continue to forty flips using the same method.
Compare the fraction for the first ten with the fraction for all forty.
expeditions.evidence: A running tally and two fractions.
expeditions.explanation: More observations can stabilize an estimate, but bias in the method does not disappear automatically.
expeditions.extension: How might a curled card affect your interpretation?
expeditions.safety: Flip over a tabletop away from faces; this is not proof that the card is fair.

expeditions.title: Mean and Median
expeditions.question: Can one unusual value change a summary?
steps: Use the invented values 2, 3, 3, 4 and 8.
Calculate the mean by adding and dividing by five; identify the median after sorting.
Replace 8 with 28 and repeat both summaries.
expeditions.evidence: Two means, two medians and an explanation.
expeditions.explanation: The mean uses every value; the median depends on middle position in sorted data. They describe different aspects.
expeditions.extension: Which summary would you choose for a typical value here, and why?
expeditions.safety: Use fictional data rather than personal finances or scores.

expeditions.title: Graph Honesty
expeditions.question: Can a graph make the same difference look larger?
steps: Graph the invented counts 90 and 100 with an axis starting at zero.
Draw a second graph with a clearly marked axis starting at eighty.
