Compare the visual impression and explain both scales.
expeditions.evidence: Two labeled graphs of identical data.
expeditions.explanation: Axis choices change appearance; clear scales help readers judge magnitude.
expeditions.extension: Which graph would you choose for a family-facing explanation?
expeditions.safety: Label invented data and avoid presenting it as a real survey.

expeditions.title: Time Budget
expeditions.question: Can a plan fit within a fixed time?
steps: Plan a thirty-minute expedition with preparation, observing, recording and cleanup.
Add your estimates and revise if the total exceeds thirty.
Try a small part and compare estimated with actual duration.
expeditions.evidence: A time budget and one measured adjustment.
expeditions.explanation: A total constraint requires tradeoffs; estimates can be improved with observations.
expeditions.extension: How much buffer would help with interruptions?
expeditions.safety: An adult approves any real outing; do not rush safety steps to meet a timer.

expeditions.title: Distance Rate Time
expeditions.question: How do speed and duration combine in a simple model?
steps: Imagine a toy traveling two grid units each second for five seconds.
Draw each second's position and calculate total distance.
Repeat at three units per second and explain the constant-speed assumption.
expeditions.evidence: Two position tables and distance calculations.
expeditions.explanation: For constant speed, distance equals speed multiplied by time; real motion can vary.
expeditions.extension: How would a two-second pause change the table?
expeditions.safety: This is an invented model, not a prediction of vehicle travel.

expeditions.title: Volume Layers
expeditions.question: How can layers help count a rectangular solid?
expeditions.materials: Large blocks or drawn cubes, paper
steps: Build or draw a base two units by three units.
Add two identical layers above it for three layers total.
Count directly and compare with length times width times height.
expeditions.evidence: A labeled model and matching cube count.
expeditions.explanation: A rectangular prism's volume can be counted by equal layers; units are cubic.
expeditions.extension: What changes if a cube is missing from one layer?
expeditions.safety: Use blocks too large to swallow or work entirely on paper.

expeditions.title: Measurement Uncertainty
expeditions.question: Why might repeated measurements differ slightly?
steps: Measure the same strip three times, resetting the ruler each time.
Ask a partner to measure it without seeing your results.
Compare the spread and discuss ruler markings and alignment.
expeditions.evidence: Repeated measurements with units and a reasonable reported length.
expeditions.explanation: Measurement has limits; reporting many digits does not automatically make a result more accurate.
expeditions.extension: What tool or method would reduce the largest uncertainty?
expeditions.safety: Use a safe ruler; no blades are required.

expeditions.title: Budget a Model
expeditions.question: Can a design meet a fictional spending limit?
steps: Set a twenty-token budget with paper costing two, tape strips one and card pieces three.
Plan a model and calculate the total.
Create another feasible plan and compare remaining tokens.
expeditions.evidence: Two itemized fictional budgets.
expeditions.explanation: A budget combines quantities and unit costs; the cheapest design may not meet the task requirements.
expeditions.extension: What if one material's cost doubles?
expeditions.safety: Use fictional tokens only; no purchasing or account information.

expeditions.title: Combination Closet
expeditions.question: How many distinct outfits can we make from choices?
steps: Draw three shirts and two hats.
List each shirt-hat pair systematically.
Add a third hat and predict the new total before listing.
expeditions.evidence: A complete pair list and counting rule.
expeditions.explanation: Independent choices multiply: each shirt can pair with each hat in this model.
expeditions.extension: What if one particular pairing is not allowed?
expeditions.safety: Use drawings rather than buying or photographing clothing.

expeditions.title: Evidence Review
expeditions.question: Which conclusion is justified by a small dataset?
steps: Use fictional ramp distances 12, 14, 13 and 15 centimeters for design A, and 13, 13, 14 and 14 for B.
Compare averages and ranges.
Write a cautious conclusion and propose another trial rather than declaring a universal winner.
expeditions.evidence: Calculations, a limited conclusion and a next-test plan.
expeditions.explanation: Similar averages can hide different spreads; a small dataset does not establish performance in all conditions.
expeditions.extension: Which new condition would most challenge your conclusion?
expeditions.safety: These are invented data for reasoning practice, not results from a tested product.
